query: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-chromium steels, a heat-treatment that induces short-range ordering leads to a more uniform distribution of Cr, which promotes the formation of a continuous, self-healing, Cr-rich passive oxide film that significantly improves corrosion resistance.
generation.material_initial_state: High-chromium steel alloy with a relatively homogeneous Cr distribution but lacking tailored short-range ordering.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled heat-treatment protocol (e.g., specific aging temperature and duration) intended to induce short-range ordering of Cr atoms within the steel matrix.
generation.conditions: Corrosion testing in environments that simulate chemical-processing and nuclear reactor conditions (for instance, exposure to saline solutions or high-temperature water with controlled chemistry).
generation.structural_mediator: Short-range ordered Cr-rich nanoclusters formed within the steel microstructure that act as nucleation sites for developing a uniform protective Cr oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: The induced short-range ordering minimizes Cr depletion sites by homogenizing the distribution of Cr, which in turn facilitates a more consistent and rapidly formed passive oxide film. This film is self-healing under mild mechanical or chemical disturbances, thus providing enhanced resistance to localized and generalized corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, heat-treated steels will exhibit faster passivation layer formation, fewer local corrosion pits, and a lower overall corrosion rate (as measured by potentiodynamic polarization and weight loss tests) under simulated service conditions.
generation.baseline: Steel samples processed with standard methods without the specific heat-treatment will have a more heterogeneous Cr distribution, resulting in slower or incomplete passivation and higher susceptibility to corrosion.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold in high-chromium steel alloys under oxidative, corrosive environments typical of chemical processing and nuclear-power applications. It may not apply to low-chromium or non-oxidizing conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative relationship between the degree of short-range ordering and the extent of corrosion resistance improvement is uncertain and could be affected by additional alloying elements and processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-chromium steel samples: one set undergoes the tailored heat-treatment to induce short-range ordering while the control set is processed via standard methods. Expose both sets to simulated chemical-processing and nuclear reactor environments (e.g., saline and high-temperature water baths). Perform time-resolved electrochemical testing and microstructural analysis (using electron diffraction or atom probe tomography) to assess passivation kinetics and uniformity.
measurements: Passivation layer formation time (measured by electrochemical impedance spectroscopy)
Corrosion rate (via potentiodynamic polarization and weight loss tests)
Microstructural characterization to quantify short-range ordering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in passivation formation speed, uniformity of the oxide layer, and lower corrosion rates compared to the untreated control, or if the degree of induced short-range ordering does not correlate with these improvements, then the hypothesis is falsified.

Microstructure, Thermal, and Corrosion Behavior of the AlAgCuNiSnTi Equiatomic Multicomponent Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe paper presents the microstructure and corrosion behavior of an AlTiNiCuAgSn new equiatomic multicomponent alloy. The alloy was obtained using the vacuum arc remelting (VAR) technique in MRF-ABJ900 equipment. The microstructural analysis was performed by optical and scanning electron microscopy (SEM microscope, SEM-EDS) and the phase transformations were highlighted by dilatometric analysis and differential thermal analysis (DTA). The results show that the as-cast alloy microstructure is three-phase, with an average microhardness of 487 HV0.1/15. The obtained alloy could be included in the group of compositionally complex alloys (CCA). The corrosion resistance was studied using the potentiodynamic method in saline solution with 3.5% NaCl. Data-driven electron-diffraction approach reveals local short-range ordering in CrCoNi with ordering effects

Abstract: The exceptional mechanical strength of medium/high-entropy alloys has been attributed to hardening in random solid solutions. Here, we evidence non-random chemical mixing in a CrCoNi alloy, resulting from short-range ordering. A data-mining approach of electron nanodiffraction enabled the study, which is assisted by neutron scattering, atom probe tomography, and diffraction simulation using first-principles theory models. Two samples, one homogenized and one heat-treated, are observed. In both samples, results reveal two types of short-range-order inside nanoclusters that minimize the Cr–Cr nearest neighbors (L12) or segregate Cr on alternating close-packed planes (L11). The L11 is predominant in the homogenized sample, while the L12 formation is promoted by heat-treatment, with the latter being accompanied by a dramatic change in dislocation-slip behavior. These findings uncover short-range order and the resulted chemical heterogeneities behind the mechanical strength in CrCoNi, providing general opportunities for atomistic-structure study in concentrated alloys
